input: Write a short thank-you speech for the award ceremony

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Knowing which award and what it recognises shapes the entire subject matter and what achievements to reference.
The specific individuals or groups to thank (colleagues, family, mentors, organisers) are the core content of any thank-you speech.
The nature and formality of the ceremony (professional gala, school event, community award, etc.) determines the register and tone.
A strict time or word limit directly controls how much can be said and how deeply each point can be developed.
The desired tone (heartfelt and emotional vs. professional and concise vs. humorous) defines the writing style throughout.
Understanding what a great speech looks like to the user — e.g., memorable closing line, specific emotional impact, audience reaction — guides prioritisation.
Whether the speech is delivered by the user themselves or written for someone else changes the voice, pronouns, and personal details needed.

gold.taskTitle: Write a short thank-you speech for award ceremony
gold.taskDescription: Write a brief thank-you speech to be delivered at an award ceremony.

questions.title: What award is being received and what does it recognise?
questions.description: Identify the name of the award and the achievement or category it honours, so the speech content is specific and relevant.

questions.title: Who specifically needs to be thanked in the speech?
questions.description: List the key people or groups — colleagues, mentors, family, sponsors, organisers — that must be acknowledged.

questions.title: What type of event or organisation is hosting the ceremony?
questions.description: Clarify whether this is a corporate, academic, community, creative industry, or other type of event to set the appropriate register.

questions.title: How long should the speech be in time or words?
questions.description: Establish a firm length target — e.g., under 1 minute, 2 minutes, 150 words — to scope the content correctly.

questions.title: What tone should the speech strike — heartfelt, professional, or humorous?
questions.description: Determine the emotional register and style the user wants to convey to the audience.

questions.title: What one feeling or message should the audience take away?
questions.description: Pinpoint the single most important impression the speech should leave — gratitude, inspiration, humility, pride — to guide emphasis and the closing line.

questions.title: Are you delivering this speech yourself or writing it for someone else?
questions.description: Establish whose voice the speech is written in, since a self-delivered speech requires personal anecdotes and first-person authenticity, while a ghostwritten one needs the recipient's details.
